title: One slow dependency is eating your whole thread pool — how do you stop it from taking everything else down?
summary: The bulkhead pattern — isolating resource pools per dependency — as distinct from a circuit breaker, which reacts to failure rather than isolating resource consumption.

slides.sectionTitle: Snapshot: why a circuit breaker alone doesn't fix this
slides.markdown:
A circuit breaker reacts to failure by stopping new calls once a dependency looks unhealthy — but it doesn't stop calls **already in flight** from holding onto shared resources while it decides. If those in-flight calls fill a shared thread pool, unrelated healthy dependencies stall too, breaker or no breaker.

The strong answer names the **bulkhead pattern**: give each dependency its own bounded resource pool, so its failure mode is capped to its own allocation.

Ask: are calls to this dependency **sharing a thread or connection pool** with calls to other, healthy dependencies? If each dependency already has its own pool, this failure mode may not even apply.

Also ask: **how many concurrent calls** does the slow dependency typically hold open when it's degraded? That number tells you roughly how much of a shared pool a single bad dependency could consume before anything else even notices.

Give each dependency its **own bounded resource pool** — threads, connections, or a semaphore — so one dependency running slow can only exhaust **its own allocation**, never the shared pool other dependencies rely on.

This is the bulkhead pattern, named after ship compartments: a hole in one compartment floods that compartment, not the whole ship.

A worked example: a service calling both a **fast internal cache** and a **slow third-party enrichment API** from the same 100-thread pool. Normally both calls return in milliseconds, so the pool has plenty of headroom.

When the enrichment API starts taking **30 seconds per call instead of 200ms**, all 100 threads fill up waiting on it — and even the cache calls, completely unrelated to the slow dependency, start queuing and timing out, because there are no free threads left to run them.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the fix — a dedicated 15-thread bulkhead
slides.markdown:
![Bulkhead thread pool split](assets/thread-pool-bulkhead.svg)

The fix: a dedicated **15-thread bulkhead** for the enrichment API calls. When it degrades, at most 15 threads get stuck waiting — the other 85 keep serving every other dependency's calls normally, completely unaffected by the enrichment API's slowdown.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: bulkheads at the connection-pool level too
slides.markdown:
The same pattern applies below the thread level: a **separate database connection pool per major query pattern or dependency** means one runaway query pattern — say, a poorly-indexed report query holding connections open for minutes — can't starve connections needed by unrelated, healthy queries hitting the same database.

Bulkheading isn't one specific mechanism — it's a principle (bound and separate resource consumption per dependency) applied wherever a shared pool exists: threads, connections, semaphores, even separate deployable services.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Bulkheads **waste some capacity by design** — the 15 threads reserved for the enrichment API sit idle when it's healthy and traffic elsewhere is heavy, capacity that a fully shared pool could have used for something else in that moment.

You're trading **maximum resource utilization** for a **hard ceiling on blast radius** — accepting some average-case waste in exchange for a guaranteed worst-case bound on how much damage one dependency can do.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you size each bulkhead's pool?
slides.markdown:
Expect: **"how do you size each bulkhead's pool?"** From the dependency's **normal concurrency needs plus enough headroom for expected load** — measure how many concurrent calls it typically needs at peak, then add margin.

Not an **even split across all dependencies** regardless of how much traffic each one actually gets — a low-traffic dependency doesn't need the same allocation as a high-traffic one, and over-allocating to every dependency equally wastes the exact capacity bulkheads are meant to protect.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: does a bulkhead replace a circuit breaker?
slides.markdown:
Expect: **"does a bulkhead replace the need for a circuit breaker on the same dependency?"** No — they solve **different problems together**: the bulkhead **caps the damage** while the dependency is failing, limiting how many resources it can consume; the circuit breaker **stops sending it calls** once it's clearly failing, so new requests don't even attempt to use the bulkhead's capacity.

Use both: the bulkhead handles calls already in flight when things go bad, the breaker prevents new calls from making it worse.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: relying on a circuit breaker alone
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have a circuit breaker on this dependency, so the shared thread pool is already protected."

**Why it's wrong:** a circuit breaker only stops **new calls** after it trips — it does nothing about calls that are **already in flight** and holding threads or connections when the dependency starts slowing down. The pool can already be exhausted by the time the breaker's failure threshold is even crossed.

**Correct model:** a circuit breaker and a bulkhead solve different halves of the problem — the breaker stops new damage, the bulkhead caps how much damage in-flight calls can do. Relying on the breaker alone leaves the shared-pool exhaustion problem completely unaddressed.

A shared thread or connection pool lets one slow dependency exhaust resources needed by unrelated, healthy dependencies. Fix: give each dependency its own bounded pool (a bulkhead), sized to its normal concurrency plus headroom, not an even split. Bulkheads waste some idle capacity by design in exchange for a hard ceiling on blast radius. Pair with a circuit breaker — the bulkhead caps in-flight damage, the breaker stops new calls.

For the full pattern and sizing guidance, see [Bulkheads and Isolation](bulkheads-and-isolation).
